_meta.generated: authored offline at build time (see scripts/generate-explanations.mjs to regenerate with a model)
_meta.note: Prose per CONCEPT and ERROR CLASS, not per item — items are infinite. Rendered instantly, no runtime LLM call.

tile.recognition.characters.core: Characters 萬 carry a numeral over a red 萬. Read the numeral, not the shape of the whole face — 四 and 西 trip beginners because both have boxy frames.
tile.recognition.characters.onError: Slow reads compound: every second spent decoding your own hand is a second not spent watching the discards.

tile.recognition.circles.core: Circles 筒 are counted, not read — the dot arrangement IS the number. Learn the layouts as shapes: 5 is a quincunx, 7 is a diagonal over a square, 9 is a 3×3 block.
tile.recognition.circles.onError: 6筒 vs 8筒 and 8筒 vs 9筒 are the classic misreads. Count columns first, then rows.

tile.recognition.bamboo.core: Bamboo 索 are counted like circles, with one exception: 1索 is the bird. If you see a bird, it's a one.
tile.recognition.bamboo.onError: 2索 vs 3索 confusions come from counting sticks instead of rows — read the row structure.

tile.recognition.honours.core: Four winds (東南西北) and three dragons (中 red, 發 green, 白 the blank frame). Honours never form chows — they only pair or pung.
tile.recognition.honours.onError: 東 (east) vs 南 (south) is a pure memorisation pair — link 東 to the sun rising behind a tree.

set.chow.core: A chow is three consecutive ranks in ONE suit. Two hard rules: no wrapping (8-9-1 is illegal) and no honours.
set.chow.onError: If your 'run' crosses suits or wraps past 9, it isn't a run — the engine will never accept it and neither will your family.

set.pung-kong.core: A pung is three identical tiles; a kong is all four, declared, and earns a replacement draw from the dead wall. Any tile kind can pung — including honours.
set.pung-kong.onError: A kong is not just a big pung: it must be declared to count, and concealed kongs score differently from exposed ones.

shape.standard.core: A winning hand is 4 sets + 1 pair = 14 tiles. If you can't carve the hand into exactly that, it doesn't win — no matter how pretty it looks.
shape.standard.onError: Near-misses are designed to fool pattern-matching. Actually decompose: find the pair, then peel off sets from the lowest tile up.

shape.decompose.core: Many hands read more than one way — 111222333 is three pungs OR three identical chows. Scoring always takes the most valuable reading, so seeing all readings is worth real faan.
shape.decompose.onError: If you got stuck, start from a different pair. The pair choice is what usually forces or frees the rest of the hand.

shape.seven-pairs.core: Seven Pairs: exactly seven DIFFERENT pairs, fully concealed. Under our rule four-of-a-kind is NOT two pairs.
shape.seven-pairs.onError: Count distinct kinds, not tiles: m1 m1 m1 m1 gives you one pair kind, not two.

shape.thirteen-orphans.core: Thirteen Orphans: one of every terminal (1 and 9 of each suit) and every honour, plus a duplicate of any of them. A limit hand — and almost always a trap to chase.
shape.thirteen-orphans.onError: Check for the missing kind first. Twelve kinds plus two duplicates is still one kind short.

faan.patterns.core: Faan come from patterns layered on the shape: suit purity, pungs vs chows, winds, dragons, and how you won. The shape wins the hand; the patterns pay for it.
faan.patterns.onError: Score what fired, not what nearly fired: a wind pung only scores if it matches your seat or the round.

faan.exclusivity.core: Superseded patterns never add: Pure One Suit replaces Mixed, Great Dragons replaces Small Dragons and its pungs, All Honours already contains All Pungs.
faan.exclusivity.onError: Double-counting is the most common scoring mistake at real tables. When a big pattern fires, ask what it swallowed.

declare.minimum.core: Below the table minimum a complete hand cannot be declared. At a 0 minimum (family rules) every complete hand wins — at 3, a bare hand must find value first.
declare.minimum.onError: 'Complete' and 'declarable' are different states. Know your table's minimum before you plan the hand.

efficiency.shanten.core: Shanten is your distance from ready: 0 means one tile away (tenpai), -1 means won. Every discard decision starts with 'what keeps my shanten lowest?'
efficiency.shanten.onError: You can't feel shanten — you count it. Sets, partial sets, and the pair; the formula does the rest.

efficiency.ukeire.core: Two discards can leave the same shanten but very different futures: ukeire counts the UNSEEN tiles that advance you. 24 live tiles beats 4 live tiles, every time.
efficiency.ukeire.onError: Subtract what you can see: copies in your hand, the pools, and melds are dead. A wait on tiles that are already visible is a wait on nothing.

efficiency.discard-choice.core: Best discard = lowest shanten first, widest wait second, safety third. Isolated honours go early; two-sided waits (like 45 waiting 3/6) are gold — never break them casually.
efficiency.discard-choice.onError: The usual leaks: hoarding isolated honours 'just in case', and trading a two-sided wait for a middle wait that looks prettier.

defence.safe-tiles.core: A tile an opponent has already discarded is safe against them. Next safest: tiles adjacent to their discards, honours with most copies visible, and suits they are clearly flooding away.
defence.safe-tiles.onError: Middle tiles (4-5-6) connect to the most waits — when in doubt, they are the most dangerous thing in your hand.

defence.push-fold.core: When an opponent is loud (2+ melds, few discards, late wall) and your hand is still 2+ from ready — fold. Feed them nothing; losing less is winning more.
defence.push-fold.onError: The expensive mistake isn't missing your win, it's paying for theirs. Count their tells before you push.

read.suit-inference.core: Players rarely throw the suit they are collecting. A pool flooded with bamboo means the bamboo in your hand is relatively safe — and their hand lives in the other suits.
read.suit-inference.onError: Read the pool as a story in draw order: early honour discards mean a normal hand; early middle-tile discards mean something shaped and dangerous.

read.threat.core: Threat = exposed melds + a short discard row + a shrinking wall. Two melds is a warning; three is a siren.
read.threat.onError: Being confidently wrong about a threat is the expensive failure — track your calibration, not just your accuracy.

errorClasses.kept-isolated-honour: You held an isolated honour over a useful suit tile. A lone wind pairs up about once in five hands — it is almost always the right first discard.
errorClasses.narrowed-wait: Same shanten, much narrower wait: you kept the hand's distance but shrank its future. Compare live-tile counts, not just shanten.
errorClasses.broke-set: That discard broke a made set or two-sided shape and moved you AWAY from ready. Count what each tile is holding together before it goes.
errorClasses.fed-the-threat: That tile was hot against the table's loudest hand. When a player is close, every unsafe discard is a bet — make it deliberately or not at all.
errorClasses.overconfident: Marked 'certain' and wrong — the most dangerous pattern at a real table. Confidence should track evidence, and the evidence is in the pools.
